title: Numbers and Sets

sources.title: Faculty of Mathematics, University of Cambridge: Schedules of Lecture Courses and Form of Examinations, Mathematical Tripos 2026-27
sources.used_for: syllabus (six schedule sections, topic order, lecture counts) and Part IA examination format; the 8-lecture elementary number theory section is split here into two topics

about: Numbers and Sets is a 24-lecture Michaelmas Term course in Part IA of the Cambridge Mathematical Tripos. Following the official schedule it covers number systems and logic, sets, relations and functions, the integers and induction, elementary number theory (Euclid's algorithm, congruences, the Chinese Remainder Theorem, Wilson and Fermat–Euler, RSA), the real numbers and countability. It is examined on Paper 4 alongside Dynamics and Relativity: each Part IA paper has a Section I of shorter questions and a Section II of longer ones, and the course is not examined for students taking Option (b), Mathematics with Physics.
topics: The integers: induction and the Binomial Theorem
Primes, highest common factors and Euclid's algorithm
Modular arithmetic, Chinese Remainder Theorem, Fermat-Euler, Wilson and RSA

notes.body:
Numbers and Sets is many students' first encounter with the Cambridge habit of proving everything. The opening lectures fix the number systems you will work in and the logical tools you need to write a correct proof.

Number systems
- ℕ = {1, 2, 3, ...} (some authors include 0; say which you mean), ℤ the integers, ℚ the rationals p/q with q ≠ 0, ℝ the reals and ℂ the complex numbers.
- A real number that is not rational is irrational, for example √2.
- A complex number is algebraic if it is a root of a non-zero polynomial with integer coefficients, e.g. √2 (root of x² − 2) and i (root of x² + 1). Otherwise it is transcendental. Every rational is algebraic (p/q is a root of qx − p).
- e and π are transcendental (proved by Hermite in 1873 and Lindemann in 1882); you need only the statements, not the proofs.
- Fundamental Theorem of Algebra (statement only): every non-constant polynomial with complex coefficients has a root in ℂ.

Statements and implication
- P ⇒ Q ("if P then Q") is false only when P is true and Q is false. So a statement with a false hypothesis is (vacuously) true.
- The converse of P ⇒ Q is Q ⇒ P; it is a different statement. The contrapositive ¬Q ⇒ ¬P is logically equivalent to P ⇒ Q.
- P ⇔ Q means both P ⇒ Q and Q ⇒ P. Prove the two directions separately.

Negation
- ¬(P and Q) is (¬P) or (¬Q); ¬(P or Q) is (¬P) and (¬Q).
- ¬(P ⇒ Q) is P and ¬Q.
- ¬(for all x, P(x)) is "there exists x with ¬P(x)", and ¬(there exists x with P(x)) is "for all x, ¬P(x)".
- Worked example: "a_n → a" means: for every ε > 0 there is N such that |a_n − a| < ε for all n ≥ N. Its negation is: there is some ε > 0 such that for every N there is an n ≥ N with |a_n − a| ≥ ε. Swap each quantifier and negate the final condition.

Methods of proof
- Direct proof: assume P, deduce Q.
- Contrapositive: to show "n² even ⇒ n even", show "n odd ⇒ n² odd": (2k + 1)² = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1.
- Contradiction: assume the statement is false and derive something impossible. The classic examples (infinitely many primes, irrationality of √2) appear later in the course.
- Counter-examples: one example disproves a "for all" statement. n² + n + 41 is prime for n = 0, 1, ..., 39, but at n = 40 it equals 41². Checking many cases is not a proof.
- Axioms: mathematics builds from stated axioms, and a proof may use only the axioms and results already proved. Later the course takes ℝ to be an ordered field satisfying the least upper bound axiom.

Common slips
- Proving the converse instead of the statement asked.
- Writing "∃N ∀n" when you mean "∀n ∃N"; the order of quantifiers changes the meaning. "For every n there is m > n" is true in ℕ; "there is m with m > n for every n" is false.

Exam tips: in Section I questions, state clearly what you assume and what you are proving, and write negations out in full rather than in your head.

This section supplies the language used in every later course: sets, functions between them and relations on them, plus some counting.

Sets
- A ∪ B (union), A ∩ B (intersection), A ∖ B (elements of A not in B), and the complement Aᶜ within a fixed universe X.
- A = B means A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A. The standard proof of a set identity shows both inclusions ("double inclusion").
- De Morgan's laws: (A ∪ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ and (A ∩ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∪ Bᶜ.
- The power set P(X) is the set of all subsets of X; if |X| = n then |P(X)| = 2ⁿ.

Indicator functions
- For A ⊆ X, the indicator function 1_A : X → {0, 1} is 1 on A and 0 off A. Two sets are equal exactly when their indicator functions are equal.
- Rules: 1_{A∩B} = 1_A·1_B, 1_{Aᶜ} = 1 − 1_A, and 1_{A∪B} = 1_A + 1_B − 1_A·1_B.
- Example: A ∩ (B ∪ C) has indicator 1_A(1_B + 1_C − 1_B1_C) = 1_A1_B + 1_A1_C − 1_A1_B1_C, which is the indicator of (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C), since 1_A² = 1_A. So the two sets are equal.

Functions
- f : A → B is injective if f(a) = f(a′) implies a = a′; surjective if every b ∈ B equals f(a) for some a; bijective if both.
- f has a two-sided inverse exactly when it is bijective. For non-empty A, f is injective if and only if it has a left inverse g (g∘f = id_A), and surjective if and only if it has a right inverse h (f∘h = id_B).
- A composition of injections is injective and of surjections is surjective. If g∘f is injective then f is injective; if g∘f is surjective then g is surjective.

Relations
- A relation on X is a subset R of X × X; write x ~ y if (x, y) ∈ R.
- It is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive (x ~ x), symmetric (x ~ y ⇒ y ~ x) and transitive (x ~ y and y ~ z ⇒ x ~ z).
- The equivalence classes [x] = {y : y ~ x} partition X: every element lies in exactly one class. Conversely every partition comes from an equivalence relation.
- Example: congruence modulo n on ℤ has n classes. "x ≤ y" on ℝ is reflexive and transitive but not symmetric.

Counting
- If |A| = m and |B| = n: there are nᵐ functions A → B, n(n − 1)...(n − m + 1) injections, and the number of k-element subsets of an n-set is C(n, k) = n!/(k!(n − k)!).
- Inclusion–Exclusion: |A₁ ∪ ... ∪ Aₙ| = Σ|Aᵢ| − Σ|Aᵢ ∩ Aⱼ| + Σ|Aᵢ ∩ Aⱼ ∩ Aₖ| − ... + (−1)ⁿ⁺¹|A₁ ∩ ... ∩ Aₙ|, the sums over i < j < k etc. A slick proof uses 1 − 1_{A₁∪...∪Aₙ} = (1 − 1_{A₁})...(1 − 1_{Aₙ}).
- Example: of 1, ..., 100, the number divisible by 2, 3 or 5 is 50 + 33 + 20 − 16 − 10 − 6 + 3 = 74.
- Surjections from a 4-set onto a 3-set: 3⁴ − 3·2⁴ + 3·1⁴ = 36. Derangements of 4 objects: 4!(1 − 1 + 1/2 − 1/6 + 1/24) = 9.

Exam tips: for an equivalence relation, check all three properties explicitly and describe the classes; in counting questions say which sets Aᵢ you are applying Inclusion–Exclusion to.

notes.h: The integers: induction and the Binomial Theorem
notes.body:
The two lectures on the integers are about the key structural property of ℕ: you cannot descend for ever. This appears in two equivalent forms, induction and well-ordering.

Mathematical induction
- Weak induction: if P(1) is true and P(n) ⇒ P(n + 1) for every n ≥ 1, then P(n) holds for all n ∈ ℕ.
- Strong induction: if P(1) holds and (P(1) and ... and P(n)) ⇒ P(n + 1), then P(n) holds for all n. Useful when the step uses earlier cases, e.g. factorisation into primes.
- Write induction proofs with a clear base case, a clearly stated inductive hypothesis, and the step.

Examples
- 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n + 1)/2. Step: n(n + 1)/2 + (n + 1) = (n + 1)(n + 2)/2.
- Bernoulli's inequality: (1 + x)ⁿ ≥ 1 + nx for x ≥ −1. Step: (1 + x)ⁿ⁺¹ ≥ (1 + nx)(1 + x) = 1 + (n + 1)x + nx² ≥ 1 + (n + 1)x, using 1 + x ≥ 0.
- 6 divides n³ − n: either note n³ − n = (n − 1)n(n + 1), a product of three consecutive integers, or by induction, since (n + 1)³ − (n + 1) = (n³ − n) + 3n(n + 1) and n(n + 1) is even.

A classic false proof
"All horses are the same colour": the step from n to n + 1 removes one horse, then another, and uses overlap. The overlap is empty when n = 1, so P(1) ⇒ P(2) fails. Always check that the step works for the smallest case it is used on.

Well-ordering principle
- Every non-empty subset of ℕ has a least element. This is equivalent to induction.
- Typical use, the "minimal counter-example": to show every integer n ≥ 2 has a prime factor, suppose not and let n be the least counter-example. n is not prime (it would be its own prime factor), so n = ab with 1 < a < n; a has a prime factor by minimality, and it divides n. Contradiction.

The Binomial Theorem
- For n ≥ 0, (a + b)ⁿ = Σₖ₌₀ⁿ C(n, k) aⁿ⁻ᵏbᵏ, valid in any commutative setting (e.g. integers, reals, integers mod m).
- Pascal's rule C(n, k) = C(n − 1, k − 1) + C(n − 1, k) drives an induction proof, and also has a counting proof: a k-subset of {1, ..., n} either contains n or does not.
- Consequences: Σₖ C(n, k) = 2ⁿ (put a = b = 1); Σₖ (−1)ᵏC(n, k) = 0 for n ≥ 1 (a = 1, b = −1).
- If p is prime and 0 < k < p then p divides C(p, k) = p!/(k!(p − k)!), because p divides the numerator but not the denominator. So (a + b)ᵖ ≡ aᵖ + bᵖ (mod p), and induction on a gives aᵖ ≡ a (mod p), one route to Fermat's little theorem.

Exam tips: in induction questions the inductive hypothesis must be exactly P(n); if the step needs more, switch to strong induction and say so.

notes.h: Primes, highest common factors and Euclid's algorithm
notes.body:
Elementary number theory has eight lectures, the largest block of the course. The first half builds from the division algorithm to unique factorisation.

Division and highest common factors
- Division algorithm: for integers a and b > 0 there are unique q, r with a = qb + r and 0 ≤ r < b.
- The highest common factor hcf(a, b) (also written gcd) is the largest positive integer dividing both. a and b are coprime if hcf(a, b) = 1.
- Key fact: if a = qb + r then hcf(a, b) = hcf(b, r), since the common divisors of a, b are exactly those of b, r.

Euclid's algorithm
- Repeat the division algorithm: divide, replace (a, b) by (b, r), and stop when the remainder is 0. The last non-zero remainder is the hcf.
- Worked example, hcf(252, 198):
  - 252 = 1 × 198 + 54
  - 198 = 3 × 54 + 36
  - 54 = 1 × 36 + 18
  - 36 = 2 × 18 + 0, so hcf = 18.
- Running it backwards: 18 = 54 − 36 = 54 − (198 − 3 × 54) = 4 × 54 − 198 = 4 × (252 − 198) − 198 = 4 × 252 − 5 × 198.

Solving ax + by = c in integers
- Bézout's lemma: there are integers x, y with ax + by = hcf(a, b). In fact hcf(a, b) is the least positive integer of the form ax + by.
- ax + by = c has an integer solution if and only if d = hcf(a, b) divides c.
- If (x₀, y₀) is one solution, all solutions are x = x₀ + (b/d)k, y = y₀ − (a/d)k for k ∈ ℤ.
- Example: 252x + 198y = 36. Double the identity above: x₀ = 8, y₀ = −10; general solution x = 8 + 11k, y = −10 − 14k.

Primes and unique factorisation
- p ≥ 2 is prime if its only positive divisors are 1 and p.
- Euclid's lemma: if p is prime and p | ab then p | a or p | b. Proof: if p ∤ a then hcf(p, a) = 1, so px + ay = 1; multiply by b: b = pbx + aby, and p divides both terms.
- Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: every n ≥ 2 is a product of primes, uniquely up to order. Existence: strong induction (or minimal counter-example). Uniqueness: if p₁...pₖ = q₁...qₗ, Euclid's lemma gives p₁ = some qⱼ; cancel and induct.
- Using factorisations: if a = Π pᵢ^aᵢ and b = Π pᵢ^bᵢ, then hcf(a, b) = Π pᵢ^min(aᵢ,bᵢ) and lcm(a, b) = Π pᵢ^max(aᵢ,bᵢ), so hcf × lcm = ab. For 252 = 2²·3²·7 and 198 = 2·3²·11: hcf = 18, lcm = 2772, and 18 × 2772 = 49896 = 252 × 198.

Infinitely many primes (Euclid)
- Suppose p₁, ..., pₖ were all the primes. N = p₁p₂...pₖ + 1 has a prime factor p, which must be some pᵢ. Then pᵢ divides N − p₁...pₖ = 1, which is impossible.
- Note N need not itself be prime: 2·3·5·7·11·13 + 1 = 30031 = 59 × 509.

Exam tips: always show every line of Euclid's algorithm and the back-substitution, then check your x and y by multiplying out. Do not use unique factorisation to prove Euclid's lemma, as the lemma is needed to prove uniqueness.

notes.h: Modular arithmetic, Chinese Remainder Theorem, Fermat-Euler, Wilson and RSA
notes.body:
The second half of the number theory block works with remainders. It ends with RSA, the course's showpiece application.

Congruences
- a ≡ b (mod n) means n | (a − b). This is an equivalence relation whose classes form ℤₙ = {0, 1, ..., n − 1}, and it respects addition and multiplication.
- a is a unit mod n (has an inverse) if and only if hcf(a, n) = 1. Find the inverse with Euclid's algorithm: ax + ny = 1 gives a⁻¹ ≡ x.
- If p is prime every non-zero class is a unit, so ℤₚ is a field. If n is composite this fails, e.g. 2 × 3 ≡ 0 (mod 6).
- Linear congruence ax ≡ b (mod n): solvable if and only if d = hcf(a, n) divides b, and then there are d solutions mod n. Example: 7x ≡ 3 (mod 26). 7 × 15 = 105 = 4 × 26 + 1, so 7⁻¹ ≡ 15 and x ≡ 45 ≡ 19 (mod 26).

Chinese Remainder Theorem
- If m and n are coprime, the system x ≡ a (mod m), x ≡ b (mod n) has a solution, unique mod mn.
- Construction: write um + vn = 1; then x = a·vn + b·um works.
- Example: x ≡ 2 (mod 3), x ≡ 3 (mod 5), x ≡ 2 (mod 7). Candidates ≡ 2 mod 7 are 2, 9, 16, 23, ...; 23 ≡ 2 (mod 3) and 23 ≡ 3 (mod 5). So x ≡ 23 (mod 105).

Fermat's little theorem and Fermat–Euler
- Euler's function φ(n) is the number of units mod n, i.e. of 1 ≤ k ≤ n with hcf(k, n) = 1. φ(p) = p − 1, φ(pᵏ) = pᵏ − pᵏ⁻¹, and φ(mn) = φ(m)φ(n) when hcf(m, n) = 1 (by the Chinese Remainder Theorem). Example: φ(36) = φ(4)φ(9) = 2 × 6 = 12.
- Fermat–Euler theorem: if hcf(a, n) = 1 then a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n). Proof: multiplication by a permutes the units u₁, ..., u_φ(n), so the product of all units is unchanged, giving a^φ(n) ≡ 1. (In Groups this is Lagrange's theorem applied to the group of units.)
- Fermat's little theorem is the case n = p: a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p) for p ∤ a.
- Example: 3¹⁰⁰ mod 7. 3⁶ ≡ 1, 100 = 96 + 4, so 3¹⁰⁰ ≡ 3⁴ = 81 ≡ 4.

Wilson's theorem
- If p is prime then (p − 1)! ≡ −1 (mod p).
- Proof: pair each of 1, ..., p − 1 with its inverse. x ≡ x⁻¹ means x² ≡ 1, so p | (x − 1)(x + 1) and x ≡ ±1. All other elements cancel in pairs, leaving 1 × (p − 1) ≡ −1.
- Check: 6! = 720 = 102 × 7 + 6 ≡ −1 (mod 7). The converse also holds: for composite n > 1, (n − 1)! is not ≡ −1.

RSA public key cryptography
- Choose large primes p ≠ q, set N = pq, so φ(N) = (p − 1)(q − 1). Choose e coprime to φ(N), and d with de ≡ 1 (mod φ(N)).
- Publish (N, e); keep d (and p, q) secret. Encrypt a message m (0 ≤ m < N) as c ≡ mᵉ (mod N); decrypt as m ≡ cᵈ (mod N).
- Why it works: de = 1 + kφ(N), so for hcf(m, N) = 1, m^de = m·(m^φ(N))ᵏ ≡ m by Fermat–Euler. (The CRT shows it works for every m.)
- Security rests on the belief that factorising N is hard: knowing p and q gives φ(N) and hence d.
- Toy example: p = 5, q = 11, N = 55, φ = 40, e = 3, d = 27 (3 × 27 = 81 ≡ 1 mod 40). m = 7 gives c = 343 mod 55 = 13, and 13²⁷ ≡ 7 (mod 55).

Exam tips: reduce exponents mod φ(n) (or p − 1) before computing, and use the CRT to split large moduli into prime-power pieces.

This section explains what is special about ℝ compared with ℚ, and introduces the sequences and series that Analysis I develops in Lent.

Least upper bounds
- S ⊆ ℝ is bounded above if there is M with x ≤ M for all x ∈ S; M is an upper bound.
- s is the least upper bound (supremum, sup S) if s is an upper bound and s ≤ M for every upper bound M. Equivalently: s is an upper bound and for every ε > 0 there is x ∈ S with x > s − ε.
- The sup need not belong to S: sup{1 − 1/n : n ∈ ℕ} = 1, which is not in the set.
- Least upper bound axiom: every non-empty subset of ℝ that is bounded above has a supremum. Together with the ordered field axioms, this characterises ℝ.
- ℚ fails this: {x ∈ ℚ : x² < 2} is bounded above in ℚ but has no rational supremum.
- Consequence (Archimedean property): ℕ is not bounded above, so 1/n → 0. Proof sketch: if s = sup ℕ, then s − 1 < n for some n ∈ ℕ, giving n + 1 > s.

Sequences and series
- aₙ → a means: for every ε > 0 there is N with |aₙ − a| < ε for all n ≥ N.
- Monotone convergence: an increasing sequence that is bounded above converges, to its supremum. Proof: let s = sup aₙ; given ε, some a_N > s − ε, and for n ≥ N, s − ε < a_N ≤ aₙ ≤ s.
- A series Σaₙ converges if its partial sums converge. A series of non-negative terms converges if and only if its partial sums are bounded.
- Example: e = Σₖ≥₀ 1/k!. The partial sums increase and are below 1 + 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + ... = 3, so the series converges.

Irrationality proofs
- √2 is irrational: suppose √2 = p/q in lowest terms. Then p² = 2q², so p is even, p = 2r, then q² = 2r², so q is even, contradicting lowest terms. (Alternatively, use unique factorisation: the power of 2 in p² is even but in 2q² is odd.)
- e is irrational: suppose e = p/q with q ≥ 1. Then x = q!(e − Σₖ₌₀^q 1/k!) is an integer, since q!e = (q − 1)!p. But x = 1/(q + 1) + 1/((q + 1)(q + 2)) + ... which is positive and less than 1/(q + 1) + 1/(q + 1)² + ... = 1/q ≤ 1. An integer strictly between 0 and 1 is impossible.

Decimal expansions
- Every real number in [0, 1) has a decimal expansion 0.d₁d₂d₃..., meaning the limit of the partial sums Σ dₖ10⁻ᵏ.
- Expansions are unique except that a terminating one also has a form ending in recurring 9s: 0.5 = 0.4999...
- A real number is rational if and only if its decimal expansion is eventually periodic. Example: 0.121212... = 12/99 = 4/33.

A transcendental number
- Liouville's idea: real algebraic numbers cannot be approximated too well by rationals. If a real number α is a root of an irreducible integer polynomial of degree d ≥ 2, there is c > 0 with |α − p/q| ≥ c/q^d for all integers p, q (q > 0).
- The number L = Σₙ≥₁ 10^(−n!) = 0.110001000... has rational approximations (its partial sums) that are far too good for any such d, so L is transcendental. Liouville proved that transcendental numbers exist, and gave the first explicit examples, in 1844; this decimal, from his 1851 paper, is usually called Liouville's constant.

Exam tips: in sup questions prove both parts (upper bound, and nothing smaller is one); in the e proof, show clearly why the tail is strictly between 0 and 1.

The final four lectures show that infinite sets come in different sizes, and give a strikingly indirect proof that transcendental numbers exist.

Definitions
- A set X is finite if it is empty or in bijection with {1, ..., n} for some n. Otherwise it is infinite.
- X is countable if it is finite or in bijection with ℕ. Equivalently, X is countable if there is an injection X → ℕ (this is the most useful test).
- X is uncountable if it is not countable.

Countable sets
- Any subset of a countable set is countable (restrict the injection).
- ℤ is countable: list it as 0, 1, −1, 2, −2, ...
- ℕ × ℕ is countable: (m, n) ↦ 2ᵐ3ⁿ is injective by unique factorisation.
- ℚ is countable: send p/q in lowest terms (q > 0) to a pair of integers, and use the above.
- A countable union of countable sets is countable: if Aₙ is listed as aₙ₁, aₙ₂, ..., then (n, k) ↦ aₙₖ is a surjection from (a subset of) ℕ × ℕ onto the union, so the union is countable. (Choosing a listing for every Aₙ simultaneously quietly uses a choice principle; this is not examined.)
- The set of algebraic numbers is countable: there are countably many integer polynomials (for each degree d, the coefficient lists inject into ℤ^(d+1)), and each non-zero polynomial has finitely many roots.

ℝ is uncountable (Cantor's diagonal argument)
- It is enough to show (0, 1) is uncountable. Suppose x₁, x₂, x₃, ... lists every number in (0, 1), with decimal expansions xₙ = 0.dₙ₁dₙ₂dₙ₃...
- Define y = 0.e₁e₂e₃... with eₙ = 5 if dₙₙ ≠ 5 and eₙ = 6 if dₙₙ = 5.
- y lies in (0, 1) and has a unique expansion (no 0s or 9s), and it differs from xₙ in the nth digit. So y is not on the list. Contradiction.
- Consequence: transcendental numbers exist, and indeed the transcendentals are uncountable, since ℝ = (algebraics in ℝ) ∪ (transcendentals) and a union of two countable sets is countable. This is the "indirect proof" in the schedule.

Power sets (Cantor's theorem)
- For any set X there is no surjection (and so no bijection) f : X → P(X).
- Proof: let A = {x ∈ X : x ∉ f(x)}. If A = f(a) for some a, then a ∈ A ⇔ a ∉ f(a) = A, a contradiction.
- So P(ℕ) is uncountable. So is the set of all sequences of 0s and 1s, which is in bijection with P(ℕ) via indicator functions.

Useful standard facts
- The set of finite subsets of ℕ is countable (a union over n of the countably many subsets of {1, ..., n}). So the set of infinite subsets of ℕ is uncountable.
- The set of all functions ℕ → ℕ is uncountable, but the set of eventually zero sequences is countable.
- To show a set is uncountable, either run a diagonal argument or inject a known uncountable set into it.

Exam tips: always say which injection or surjection you use and why it is one; for uncountability, either quote a standard result clearly or give the diagonal argument in full.

cards.f: Negation of 'for all ε > 0 there is N with |aₙ − a| < ε for all n ≥ N'
cards.b: There is ε > 0 such that for every N there is some n ≥ N with |aₙ − a| ≥ ε.
Every non-constant polynomial with complex coefficients has at least one root in ℂ. Only the statement is in Numbers and Sets.
1_{A∩B} = 1_A·1_B, 1_{Aᶜ} = 1 − 1_A, 1_{A∪B} = 1_A + 1_B − 1_A·1_B. Sets are equal iff their indicator functions are equal.

f : A → B has a left inverse g : B → A with g∘f = id_A.

cards.f: Number of injections from an m-set to an n-set (m ≤ n)
Number of surjections from a 4-set onto a 3-set
cards.b: 3⁴ − 3·2⁴ + 3·1⁴ = 81 − 48 + 3 = 36 (Inclusion–Exclusion over the missed values).

cards.f: If g∘f is injective, what follows?
cards.b: f is injective (g need not be). If g∘f is surjective, then g is surjective (f need not be).
Every non-empty subset of ℕ has a least element. It is equivalent to the principle of induction.
If P(1) holds and P(1), ..., P(n) together imply P(n + 1) for each n, then P(n) holds for all n ∈ ℕ.
C(n, k) = C(n − 1, k − 1) + C(n − 1, k) for 1 ≤ k ≤ n − 1: a k-subset of {1, ..., n} either contains n or does not.
(1 + x)ⁿ ≥ 1 + nx for all n ∈ ℕ and real x ≥ −1; proved by induction using 1 + x ≥ 0.

cards.f: Why does p divide C(p, k) for prime p and 0 < k < p?
cards.b: C(p, k) = p!/(k!(p − k)!) is an integer; p divides the numerator but no factor of k!(p − k)! since all are < p.

cards.f: Where does the 'all horses are one colour' induction fail?
cards.b: The step from n = 1 to n = 2: the two overlapping groups of size n share no horse, so nothing links their colours.

cards.f: Σₖ C(n, k) and Σₖ (−1)ᵏ C(n, k)
cards.b: 2ⁿ (put a = b = 1 in the Binomial Theorem) and 0 for n ≥ 1 (put a = 1, b = −1).
For integers a and b > 0 there are unique integers q, r with a = qb + r and 0 ≤ r < b.
For integers a, b not both zero there are integers x, y with ax + by = hcf(a, b); found by running Euclid's algorithm backwards.

cards.f: When does ax + by = c have integer solutions?
cards.b: Exactly when hcf(a, b) divides c. With d = hcf, all solutions are x₀ + (b/d)k, y₀ − (a/d)k for k ∈ ℤ.
If p is prime and p | ab, then p | a or p | b. Proof uses Bézout: if p ∤ a, px + ay = 1, so b = pbx + aby.
Every integer n ≥ 2 is a product of primes, and this factorisation is unique up to the order of the factors.
= ab for positive integers a, b (compare exponents: min + max = sum).

cards.f: Euclid's proof of infinitely many primes
cards.b: If p₁, ..., pₖ were all the primes, a prime factor of p₁...pₖ + 1 would be some pᵢ, which would then divide 1.

cards.f: When is a a unit modulo n?
cards.b: Exactly when hcf(a, n) = 1. The inverse comes from ax + ny = 1, giving a⁻¹ ≡ x (mod n).
If hcf(m, n) = 1, then x ≡ a (mod m), x ≡ b (mod n) has a solution, unique modulo mn.
If hcf(a, n) = 1 then a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n), where φ(n) counts the units mod n.
If p is prime, (p − 1)! ≡ −1 (mod p). Elements pair off with their inverses; only ±1 are self-inverse.
12: φ(4)φ(9) = 2 × 6, using multiplicativity for coprime factors and φ(pᵏ) = pᵏ − pᵏ⁻¹.

cards.f: RSA: how is the decryption exponent d chosen?
cards.b: d satisfies de ≡ 1 (mod φ(N)), where N = pq and φ(N) = (p − 1)(q − 1). Then (mᵉ)ᵈ ≡ m (mod N).
4. By Fermat 3⁶ ≡ 1, and 100 = 6 × 16 + 4, so 3¹⁰⁰ ≡ 3⁴ = 81 ≡ 4.

cards.f: When is ax ≡ b (mod n) solvable?
cards.b: Exactly when d = hcf(a, n) divides b; there are then d solutions modulo n.
s = sup S if s is an upper bound of S and s ≤ M for every upper bound M; equivalently for every ε > 0 some x ∈ S has x > s − ε.
Every non-empty subset of ℝ that is bounded above has a least upper bound in ℝ.

cards.f: A bounded set in ℚ with no rational supremum
cards.b: {x ∈ ℚ : x² < 2}: its supremum in ℝ is √2, which is irrational.
An increasing sequence that is bounded above converges, and its limit is the supremum of its terms.

cards.f: Key step in proving e irrational
cards.b: If e = p/q, then q!(e − Σₖ≤q 1/k!) is an integer, but it equals 1/(q+1) + 1/((q+1)(q+2)) + ... which lies strictly between 0 and 1/q ≤ 1.

cards.f: Which reals have eventually periodic decimal expansions?
cards.b: Exactly the rationals. E.g. 0.121212... = 12/99 = 4/33.
Σ 10^(−n!) = 0.110001000000000000000001...; it is approximated too well by rationals to be algebraic, so it is transcendental.
A set that is finite or in bijection with ℕ; equivalently, a set with an injection into ℕ.

cards.f: Injection showing ℕ × ℕ is countable
cards.b: (m, n) ↦ 2ᵐ3ⁿ, injective by unique prime factorisation.

cards.f: Why are the algebraic numbers countable?
cards.b: Countably many integer polynomials (countably many for each degree) and each non-zero one has finitely many roots: a countable union of finite sets.
For any set X there is no surjection X → P(X). Take A = {x : x ∉ f(x)}; A = f(a) gives a ∈ A ⇔ a ∉ A.

cards.f: Diagonal argument: why use digits 5 and 6?
cards.b: So the new number has no 0s or 9s, hence a unique decimal expansion; it cannot equal a listed number via a 0.4999... = 0.5 coincidence.

cards.f: Is the set of finite subsets of ℕ countable?
cards.b: Yes: it is the union over n of the finite sets P({1, ..., n}). Hence the infinite subsets of ℕ form an uncountable set.
ℝ is uncountable but the algebraic numbers are countable, so ℝ contains (uncountably many) non-algebraic numbers.

questions.q: Which statement is logically equivalent to 'if n² is even then n is even'?
options: If n is odd then n² is odd
If n is even then n² is even
If n² is odd then n is odd
n² is even and n is odd
questions.why: 'If n is odd then n² is odd' is the contrapositive (not Q ⇒ not P), which is always equivalent to the original. 'If n is even then n² is even' is the converse, a different statement; 'if n² is odd then n is odd' is the inverse, equivalent to the converse; and 'n² even and n odd' is the negation of the original.

questions.q: Which of these is the negation of 'for every x ∈ ℝ there exists y ∈ ℝ with y > x'?
options: There exists x ∈ ℝ such that y ≤ x for every y ∈ ℝ
For every x ∈ ℝ there exists y ∈ ℝ with y ≤ x
There exists y ∈ ℝ with y > x for every x ∈ ℝ
For every x and y in ℝ, y ≤ x
questions.why: Negating swaps each quantifier and negates the inner condition: 'for all x, exists y, y > x' becomes 'exists x, for all y, y ≤ x'. Keeping 'for every x' but changing only the inequality does not negate the statement; 'there exists y with y > x for every x' changes the quantifier order but not the condition; and 'for all x and y, y ≤ x' is stronger than the negation.

questions.q: Explain why checking that n² + n + 41 is prime for n = 0, 1, ..., 39 does not prove it is prime for all n ≥ 0, and find a counter-example. What does this illustrate about proofs?
markScheme: States that finitely many cases cannot establish a 'for all n' claim
Gives n = 40 (or n = 41) as a counter-example
Comments that one counter-example disproves a universal statement, while a proof must cover every case
questions.modelAnswer: A statement about all n ≥ 0 is only established by an argument valid for every n; checking 40 cases says nothing about the 41st. Indeed at n = 40 we get 40² + 40 + 41 = 40(40 + 1) + 41 = 41 × 40 + 41 = 41², which is not prime (n = 41 also fails: 41(41 + 1 + 1) = 41 × 43). This shows the asymmetry between proof and disproof: one counter-example is enough to refute a universal claim, whereas evidence from many examples is never a proof.

questions.q: Which relation on ℤ is an equivalence relation?
options: x ~ y if x − y is divisible by 4
questions.why: Divisibility of x − y by 4 is reflexive, symmetric and transitive (congruence mod 4), giving four classes. 'x ≤ y' is not symmetric. '|x − y| ≤ 1' is not transitive (0 ~ 1 and 1 ~ 2 but 0 is not related to 2). 'xy > 0' fails reflexivity at 0, since 0 × 0 = 0.

questions.q: How many integers from 1 to 100 inclusive are divisible by at least one of 2, 3 and 5?
questions.why: Inclusion–Exclusion gives 50 + 33 + 20 − 16 − 10 − 6 + 3 = 74. 103 is the plain sum 50 + 33 + 20 with no corrections; 26 is the number divisible by none of them (100 − 74); 71 comes from subtracting the pairwise overlaps but forgetting to add back the 3 multiples of 30.

questions.q: Let f : A → B and g : B → C. Prove that if g∘f is injective then f is injective. Give an example showing g need not be injective.
markScheme: Assumes f(a) = f(a′) and applies g to get g(f(a)) = g(f(a′))
Uses injectivity of g∘f to deduce a = a′
Concludes f is injective
Gives a valid example, e.g. A = {1}, B = {1, 2}, C = {1}, with f(1) = 1 and g constant
Checks in the example that g∘f is injective while g is not
questions.modelAnswer: Suppose f(a) = f(a′). Applying g gives (g∘f)(a) = g(f(a)) = g(f(a′)) = (g∘f)(a′). Since g∘f is injective, a = a′. Hence f is injective. For the example, let A = {1}, B = {1, 2}, C = {1}, f(1) = 1, and g(1) = g(2) = 1. Then g∘f : {1} → {1} is injective (any function on a one-element set is), but g is not injective since g(1) = g(2) with 1 ≠ 2.

questions.q: In a proof by induction that 3ⁿ ≥ 2n + 1 for all n ≥ 1, the inductive step assumes 3ⁿ ≥ 2n + 1. Which line correctly completes the step?
questions.why: Multiplying the hypothesis by 3 gives 3ⁿ⁺¹ ≥ 6n + 3, and 6n + 3 ≥ 2n + 3 = 2(n + 1) + 1, completing the step. Writing 3ⁿ⁺¹ = 3ⁿ + 3 is false algebra; '3ⁿ⁺¹ ≥ 3ⁿ' only gives 3ⁿ⁺¹ ≥ 2n + 1, which is too weak; and 3(2n + 1) = 6n + 3 is not equal to 2n + 3.

questions.q: For a prime p, which congruence follows from the Binomial Theorem and the fact that p divides C(p, k) for 0 < k < p?
options: (a + b)ᵖ ≡ aᵖ + bᵖ (mod p), but only when p does not divide ab
questions.why: All the middle binomial coefficients C(p, k), 0 < k < p, vanish mod p, leaving only the aᵖ and bᵖ terms, and this holds for all integers a, b. '≡ 0' comes from treating the end coefficients C(p, 0) = C(p, p) = 1 as divisible by p too; the fact only covers 0 < k < p. '≡ 1' misapplies Fermat's little theorem with exponent p instead of p − 1 (try a = b = 1: 2ᵖ ≡ 2, not 1). Adding 'only when p does not divide ab' imports the coprimality hypothesis of Fermat's little theorem, but the binomial argument needs no such condition (e.g. a = p gives (p + b)ᵖ ≡ bᵖ ≡ aᵖ + bᵖ).

questions.q: Use the well-ordering principle to prove that every integer n ≥ 2 can be written as a product of primes.
markScheme: Supposes the set S of integers ≥ 2 with no prime factorisation is non-empty
Takes its least element m by well-ordering
Notes m is not prime, so m = ab with 1 < a, b < m
Uses minimality to factorise a and b into primes
Concatenates to factorise m, contradiction, so S is empty
questions.modelAnswer: Let S be the set of integers n ≥ 2 that are not products of primes, and suppose S is non-empty. By the well-ordering principle S has a least element m. m is not prime, since a prime is a product of one prime. So m = ab with 1 < a < m and 1 < b < m. As a and b are smaller than m and at least 2, they are not in S, so each is a product of primes. Then m = ab is a product of primes, contradicting m ∈ S. Hence S is empty and every n ≥ 2 is a product of primes.

questions.q: What is hcf(1071, 462)?
questions.why: Euclid: 1071 = 2 × 462 + 147, 462 = 3 × 147 + 21, 147 = 7 × 21, so the hcf is the last non-zero remainder, 21. 7 is the final quotient (147 = 7 × 21), the slip of reading off a quotient instead of the remainder; 3 is a common divisor but not the highest (it divides 21); 42 = 2 × 21 does not divide 1071, which is odd.

questions.q: For which value of c does 12x + 18y = c have integer solutions?
questions.why: Solutions exist exactly when hcf(12, 18) = 6 divides c. 6 divides 30 (e.g. x = −1, y = 1 gives 6, so x = −5, y = 5 gives 30). None of 4, 9 or 14 is a multiple of 6, so those equations have no integer solutions.

questions.q: Use Euclid's algorithm to find hcf(252, 198), express it as 252x + 198y, and find all integer solutions of 252x + 198y = 36.
markScheme: hcf = 18
Back-substitution to 18 = 4 × 252 − 5 × 198
Particular solution x = 8, y = −10 for c = 36
General solution x = 8 + 11k, y = −10 − 14k (k ∈ ℤ), with justification that these are all

questions.q: What is the remainder when 2¹⁰⁰ is divided by 13?
questions.why: By Fermat, 2¹² ≡ 1 (mod 13); 100 = 12 × 8 + 4, so 2¹⁰⁰ ≡ 2⁴ = 16 ≡ 3. The answer 1 assumes Fermat gives 2¹⁰⁰ ≡ 1 directly, which would need 100 to be a multiple of 12. 9 is 2⁸ mod 13 (256 = 19 × 13 + 9): it comes from using the quotient 8 in 100 = 12 × 8 + 4 instead of the remainder 4. 5 comes from reducing the exponent mod 13 instead of mod 12 (100 = 7 × 13 + 9, and 2⁹ = 512 = 39 × 13 + 5).

questions.q: In RSA with N = 55 and public exponent e = 3, what is the private exponent d?
questions.why: φ(55) = 4 × 10 = 40, and d must satisfy 3d ≡ 1 (mod 40); 3 × 27 = 81 = 2 × 40 + 1. Taking 37 solves 3d ≡ 1 mod 55 instead (3 × 37 = 111 = 2 × 55 + 1), the classic slip of working mod N rather than φ(N). 13 comes from dropping the sign when back-substituting 40 = 13 × 3 + 1: in fact 1 = 40 − 13 × 3, so d ≡ −13 ≡ 27 (3 × 13 = 39 ≡ −1). 3 just reuses the public exponent e as d (3 × 3 = 9, not ≡ 1 mod 40).

questions.q: State and prove Wilson's theorem.
markScheme: Statement: p prime ⇒ (p − 1)! ≡ −1 (mod p)
Each of 1, ..., p − 1 has an inverse mod p, as p is prime
x ≡ x⁻¹ ⇒ x² ≡ 1 ⇒ p | (x − 1)(x + 1) ⇒ x ≡ ±1 (Euclid's lemma)
Remaining elements cancel in inverse pairs, so (p − 1)! ≡ 1 × (p − 1) ≡ −1
Handles p = 2 separately (1! = 1 ≡ −1 mod 2)
questions.modelAnswer: Wilson's theorem: if p is prime then (p − 1)! ≡ −1 (mod p). Proof: for p = 2, 1! = 1 ≡ −1 (mod 2). Let p be odd. Since p is prime, each x ∈ {1, ..., p − 1} has a unique inverse in this set. If x is its own inverse then x² ≡ 1, so p | (x − 1)(x + 1), and by Euclid's lemma x ≡ 1 or x ≡ −1 ≡ p − 1. These are distinct as p > 2. Every other element pairs with a different element, its inverse, and each pair multiplies to 1. So (p − 1)! ≡ 1 × (p − 1) × 1 × ... × 1 ≡ −1 (mod p).

questions.q: Let S = {1 − 1/n : n ∈ ℕ}. Which is true?
options: S has no supremum because it has no largest element
questions.why: Every element is below 1, and for any ε > 0 some 1 − 1/n exceeds 1 − ε, so sup S = 1; but 1 − 1/n = 1 has no solution, so 1 ∉ S. The claim that S has no supremum confuses a supremum with a maximum (the least upper bound axiom guarantees a supremum); 1/2 is just the element given by n = 2, not an upper bound.

questions.q: Which number is rational?
questions.why: An eventually periodic decimal is rational: this one is 1/7. √2 is irrational; the decimal with ever-longer blocks of zeros never becomes periodic, so it is irrational; and Liouville's number Σ10^(−n!) is not periodic either, and is in fact transcendental.

questions.q: Prove that e = Σₖ≥₀ 1/k! is irrational.
markScheme: Assumes e = p/q with integers p, q ≥ 1
Defines x = q!(e − Σₖ₌₀^q 1/k!) and shows it is an integer
Writes x = Σₖ>q q!/k! > 0
Concludes 0 < x < 1 is impossible for an integer
questions.modelAnswer: Suppose e = p/q with p, q positive integers. Let x = q!(e − Σₖ₌₀^q 1/k!). Then q!e = (q − 1)!p is an integer and each q!/k! with k ≤ q is an integer, so x is an integer. But x = Σₖ>q q!/k! = 1/(q + 1) + 1/((q + 1)(q + 2)) + ..., so x > 0. Each term 1/((q + 1)...(q + j)) ≤ 1/(q + 1)ʲ, with strict inequality for j ≥ 2, so x < Σⱼ≥₁ (q + 1)⁻ʲ = 1/q ≤ 1. An integer strictly between 0 and 1 cannot exist, a contradiction. So e is irrational.

questions.q: Which set is uncountable?
options: The set of all subsets of ℕ
The set of finite subsets of ℕ
questions.why: By Cantor's theorem there is no surjection ℕ → P(ℕ), so P(ℕ) is uncountable. ℚ × ℚ is a product of two countable sets, hence countable; the algebraic numbers are a countable union of finite root sets; and the finite subsets of ℕ are a countable union of finite sets P({1, ..., n}).

questions.q: In Cantor's proof that f : X → P(X) cannot be surjective, which set is shown to lie outside the image of f?
questions.why: If A = {x : x ∉ f(x)} equalled f(a), then a ∈ A would hold exactly when a ∉ A. The set {x : x ∈ f(x)} gives no contradiction; X and the empty set can perfectly well be values of f (for example f could map some point to X).

questions.q: Show that a countable union of countable sets is countable, and deduce that ℚ is countable.
markScheme: Lists each Aₙ as aₙ₁, aₙ₂, ... (with repeats allowed if finite)
Defines a surjection from ℕ × ℕ (or a subset) onto the union, (n, k) ↦ aₙₖ
Shows ℕ × ℕ is countable, e.g. via (m, n) ↦ 2ᵐ3ⁿ
Concludes the union is countable (image of a countable set)
Writes ℚ as the union over q ∈ ℕ of {p/q : p ∈ ℤ}, each countable
questions.modelAnswer: Let A₁, A₂, ... be countable (we may assume non-empty). List each as Aₙ = {aₙ₁, aₙ₂, ...}, repeating elements if Aₙ is finite. The map g : ℕ × ℕ → ∪Aₙ, g(n, k) = aₙₖ, is surjective. ℕ × ℕ is countable because (m, n) ↦ 2ᵐ3ⁿ is injective (unique factorisation). A surjective image of a countable set is countable: for each y in the union, pick the (n, k) with g(n, k) = y and least 2ⁿ3ᵏ; this gives an injection of the union into ℕ. So the union is countable. For ℚ, write ℚ = ∪_{q∈ℕ} Bq with Bq = {p/q : p ∈ ℤ}; each Bq is the image of ℤ, which is countable, so ℚ is countable.

questions.q:
(a) Use Euclid's algorithm to find integers x, y with 252x + 198y = hcf(252, 198), and find all integer solutions of 252x + 198y = 36. [6]
(b) Find all integers x with x ≡ 2 (mod 3), x ≡ 3 (mod 5) and x ≡ 2 (mod 7). [4]
(c) State the Fermat–Euler theorem. In an RSA system the public key is N = 55, e = 3. Find the private exponent d, and decrypt the ciphertext c = 13, showing your working without a calculator. [10]
markScheme: (a) Euclid's algorithm steps giving hcf = 18; back-substitution 18 = 4 × 252 − 5 × 198
(a) Solution set x = 8 + 11k, y = −10 − 14k with justification
(b) Correct method (CRT or sieving) and answer x ≡ 23 (mod 105)
(c) Statement: hcf(a, n) = 1 ⇒ a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n)
(c) φ(55) = 40 and d = 27 from 3d ≡ 1 (mod 40)
(c) Reduces 13²⁷ mod 5 to 2 using 3⁴ ≡ 1
(c) Reduces 13²⁷ mod 11 to 7 using 2¹⁰ ≡ 1
(c) Combines by CRT to m = 7 and checks 7³ = 343 ≡ 13 (mod 55)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) 252 = 1 × 198 + 54; 198 = 3 × 54 + 36; 54 = 1 × 36 + 18; 36 = 2 × 18. So hcf = 18, and back-substituting, 18 = 54 − 36 = 4 × 54 − 198 = 4 × 252 − 5 × 198, so x = 4, y = −5. Doubling, (8, −10) solves 252x + 198y = 36. If (x, y) is any solution then 14(x − 8) = −11(y + 10), and since hcf(14, 11) = 1, x = 8 + 11k, y = −10 − 14k for some k ∈ ℤ; all such pairs work.

(b) 3, 5, 7 are pairwise coprime, so by the Chinese Remainder Theorem there is a unique solution mod 105. Numbers ≡ 2 (mod 7): 2, 9, 16, 23, ... 23 = 7 × 3 + 2, 23 = 3 × 7 + 2 ≡ 2 (mod 3) and 23 = 4 × 5 + 3 ≡ 3 (mod 5). So x ≡ 23 (mod 105), i.e. x = 23 + 105k.

(c) Fermat–Euler: if hcf(a, n) = 1 then a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n), φ(n) being the number of units modulo n. Here N = 5 × 11, so φ(N) = 4 × 10 = 40. We need 3d ≡ 1 (mod 40): 3 × 27 = 81 = 2 × 40 + 1, so d = 27. To decrypt, compute m ≡ 13²⁷ (mod 55) by working mod 5 and mod 11. Mod 5: 13 ≡ 3, and 3⁴ ≡ 1, so 3²⁷ = 3²⁴ × 3³ ≡ 27 ≡ 2. Mod 11: 13 ≡ 2 and 2¹⁰ ≡ 1, so 2²⁷ ≡ 2⁷ = 128 = 11 × 11 + 7 ≡ 7. Now m ≡ 7 (mod 11) and m ≡ 2 (mod 5): candidates 7, 18, 29, 40, 51, and 7 ≡ 2 (mod 5). So m = 7. Check: 7³ = 343 = 6 × 55 + 13, so encrypting 7 does give 13.

questions.q:
(a) Define what it means for a set to be countable. Prove that ℕ × ℕ is countable and that a countable union of countable sets is countable. [6]
(b) Prove that the set of real algebraic numbers is countable and that ℝ is uncountable. Deduce that transcendental numbers exist. [8]
(c) Prove that for any set X there is no bijection between X and its power set. Is the set of all infinite subsets of ℕ countable? Justify your answer. [6]
markScheme: (a) Definition: finite or in bijection with ℕ (equivalently, injects into ℕ); injection (m, n) ↦ 2ᵐ3ⁿ
(a) Union argument via surjection from ℕ × ℕ
(b) Integer polynomials of degree ≤ d inject into ℤ^(d+1); countably many polynomials, finitely many roots each
(b) Diagonal argument on (0, 1) with digits avoiding 0 and 9
(b) Deduction: ℝ = algebraic ∪ transcendental, so transcendentals non-empty (indeed uncountable)
(c) Cantor: A = {x : x ∉ f(x)} not in image
(c) Finite subsets countable; P(ℕ) uncountable; so infinite subsets uncountable
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) X is countable if it is finite or there is a bijection ℕ → X; equivalently there is an injection X → ℕ. The map ℕ × ℕ → ℕ, (m, n) ↦ 2ᵐ3ⁿ, is injective by uniqueness of prime factorisation, so ℕ × ℕ is countable. If A₁, A₂, ... are countable and non-empty, list Aₙ = {aₙ₁, aₙ₂, ...} (repeating if finite). Then (n, k) ↦ aₙₖ maps ℕ × ℕ onto ∪Aₙ. Sending each y in the union to the least 2ⁿ3ᵏ with aₙₖ = y gives an injection into ℕ, so the union is countable.

(b) For each d ≥ 1, the non-zero integer polynomials of degree d correspond to coefficient lists in ℤ^(d+1), which is countable (finite products of countable sets are countable). So the set of all non-zero integer polynomials is a countable union of countable sets, hence countable. Each has at most d real roots, so the real algebraic numbers form a countable union of finite sets: countable.
Suppose (0, 1) were countable, listed as x₁, x₂, ... with xₙ = 0.dₙ₁dₙ₂... Define y = 0.e₁e₂... with eₙ = 5 if dₙₙ ≠ 5 and eₙ = 6 otherwise. y ∈ (0, 1), and as its digits avoid 0 and 9 its expansion is unique; it differs from xₙ in the nth place, so y ≠ xₙ for every n. Contradiction, so (0, 1), and hence ℝ, is uncountable. If every real were algebraic, ℝ would be countable; so transcendental reals exist. Indeed ℝ minus the algebraics must be uncountable, as a union of two countable sets is countable.

(c) Let f : X → P(X) be any function and A = {x ∈ X : x ∉ f(x)}. If A = f(a) for some a, then a ∈ A ⇔ a ∉ f(a) ⇔ a ∉ A, a contradiction. So f is not surjective, and in particular not a bijection. Hence P(ℕ) is uncountable. The finite subsets of ℕ form the union over n of P({1, ..., n}), a countable union of finite sets, so they are countable. If the infinite subsets were also countable, P(ℕ) would be the union of two countable sets, hence countable, which is false. So the set of infinite subsets of ℕ is uncountable.
